analysis.investment_thesis: Avalon is a B2B contract electronics manufacturer with erratic earnings, consistently negative free cash flow, and a 10.4% ROE trading at 77x earnings — a combination I find deeply unattractive. At INR 7,473 Cr market cap for a business generating INR 63 Cr net profit, the market is pricing in perfection that the financials do not support.
key_strengths: Debt reduction trend: Borrowings fell from INR 274 Cr (2020) to INR 163 Cr (2025), D/E now 0.25
Revenue CAGR of 11.3% over 5 years falls within my preferred 10–15% steady-growth band
Diversified end-markets (clean energy, aerospace, railways) reduce single-client concentration risk
key_risks: Chronically negative FCF: Free cash flow negative in 4 of last 5 years (peaked at -41 Cr in FY23); a business that cannot convert profits to cash is not a real compounder
Earnings are dangerously volatile: Net profit swung 28 Cr → 63 Cr in consecutive years, and EBITDA collapsed from INR 111 Cr (FY23) to INR 66 Cr (FY24) — I cannot rely on this
Promoter holding at 44.42% is well below my 55% floor — I need the owner to be deeply invested alongside me
red_flags: P/E of 77.8x for a 10.4% ROE business is indefensible — I pay 12–20x for quality, not 78x for mediocrity
ROE at 10.4% is far below my 15% minimum; the business is not earning enough on equity to justify its premium
No dividend paid — confirms earnings are not translating to real, distributable cash
OCF of only INR 25 Cr in FY25 on INR 1,098 Cr revenue signals severe working capital drag typical of EMS businesses
Large equity raise in FY23 (equity surged INR 87 Cr → INR 537 Cr, likely IPO) diluted existing owners and is still not generating adequate returns on that capital
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Avalon is an EMS (Electronic Manufacturing Services) company — a contract assembler for other companies' products. This is structurally the wrong kind of business for me. EMS is capital-intensive, margin-thin, and carries no brand or pricing power. The gross margin of 33.8% sounds reasonable but shrinks to a 9.6% operating margin after overheads, and then nearly evaporates after capex — hence the persistently negative free cash flow. A business that earns INR 63 Cr in net profit but spends INR 46 Cr on capex and generates only INR 25 Cr in operating cash flow is running a treadmill, not building wealth for shareholders.

The valuation is the final nail. At 77.8x trailing P/E and 52x EV/EBITDA, the market is treating this like a high-quality software compounder. But Avalon's ROE is 10.4% — below what I can earn in a fixed deposit adjusted for risk. The IPO-era capital has not been put to work effectively: equity quadrupled from FY22 to FY23 (INR 87 Cr → INR 537 Cr) yet FY25 net profit is only INR 63 Cr. That is a poor return on fresh capital. I built DMart on the principle that boring businesses with disciplined capital allocation and predictable cash generation create wealth. Avalon has none of those qualities at this price.
